en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 23.1 (SN 23.1, PTS SN iii 189) 1. The First Chapter on Māra: The Discourse on Māra At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, this body is like Māra’s bait. It is not by means of this body that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, would declare himself to be fully enlightened. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or examined by the mind—all that he has fully understood. Therefore, bhikkhus, an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge, does not declare himself to be fully enlightened by means of this body, which is like Māra’s bait. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘This body is like Māra’s bait. Venerable sir, there was once a certain bhikkhu who was sick, afflicted, gravely ill. He told me: ‘Friend Ānanda, if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would visit me even for the sake of a brief conversation, it would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time. Venerable sir, I went to the Blessed One, approached him, and reported this matter to him. Then the Blessed One told me: ‘Go, Ānanda, tell that bhikkhu: “Friend, the Teacher calls you; the Blessed One calls you. ‘“Very well, venerable sir,” I replied, and I went to that bhikkhu and said: ‘“Friend, the Teacher calls you; the Blessed One calls you. ‘“When I had spoken thus, friend Ānanda, that bhikkhu said to me: ‘Do not trouble the Blessed One, friend Ānanda, do not weary the Blessed One. The Blessed One is tired. Friend Ānanda, for a second time I went to the Blessed One and reported this matter to him. And for a second time the Blessed One told me: ‘Go, Ānanda, tell that bhikkhu: “Friend, the Teacher calls you; the Blessed One calls you. ‘“For a second time, friend Ānanda, that bhikkhu said to me: ‘Do not trouble the Blessed One, friend Ānanda, do not weary the Blessed One. The Blessed One is tired. Friend Ānanda, for a third time I went to the Blessed One and reported this matter to him. And for a third time the Blessed One told me: ‘Go, Ānanda, tell that bhikkhu: “Friend, the Teacher calls you; the Blessed One calls you. ‘“For a third time, friend Ānanda, that bhikkhu said to me: ‘Do not trouble the Blessed One, friend Ānanda, do not weary the Blessed One. The Blessed One is tired. Then, friend Ānanda, I thought: ‘The Blessed One has commanded me three times, and that bhikkhu refuses to come. What can I do now? Then the Blessed One told me: ‘Ānanda, go to that bhikkhu and take hold of him by the arm and bring him to the Blessed One, even if he struggles. ‘“‘Very well, venerable sir,’ I replied, and I went to that bhikkhu and took hold of him by the arm and brought him to the Blessed One, even though he struggled. Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened that bhikkhu with a Dhamma talk. Having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a Dhamma talk, that bhikkhu’s affliction subsided right there. As one freed from fever, he sat there happy. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus, this body is like Māra’s bait. It is not by means of this body that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge, would declare himself to be fully enlightened. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... all that he has fully understood. Therefore, bhikkhus, an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant... does not declare himself to be fully enlightened by means of this body, which is like Māra’s bait. “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘This body is like Māra’s bait. Venerable sir, suppose there were a baited trap set in an empty forest, and a deer coming from the east, west, north, or south would see it and think:

‘This is a baited trap set in an empty forest; whoever comes near this will meet with death or deadly suffering. Just so, venerable sir, this body is like Māra’s bait. It is not by means of this body that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant... would declare himself to be fully enlightened. Why is that? Because, venerable sir, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... all that he has fully understood. Therefore, venerable sir, an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant... does not declare himself to be fully enlightened by means of this body, which is like Māra’s bait. “Ānanda, this body is like Māra’s bait. It is not by means of this body that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, would declare himself to be fully enlightened. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or examined by the mind—all that he has fully understood. Therefore, Ānanda, an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge, does not declare himself to be fully enlightened by means of this body, which is like Māra’s bait. “Venerable sir, it is as if there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and someone were to come along bringing a saw. He would cut down the great tree at its foot and cut off the top. Having done so, he would split the trunk into planks. From the planks he would have stakes made, and from the stakes small pieces. Then, having taken a small piece, he would go to an empty forest and set it up there. He would think: ‘This great tree that stood possessed of heartwood—this very thing is its heartwood! In the same way, venerable sir, when the Blessed One says: ‘This body is like Māra’s bait. It is not by means of this body that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant... would declare himself to be fully enlightened,’ it is as if he were taking a small piece from the great tree and setting it up in an empty forest. For, venerable sir, the Blessed One has declared: ‘Whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... all that he has fully understood. “Ānanda, it is not because of this body that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, would declare himself to be fully enlightened. But, Ānanda, it is by means of that other body—the body of the Tathāgata—that an ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, would declare himself to be fully enlightened. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or examined by
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Rādha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Rādha said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Māra, Māra,’ it is said, Bhante.”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one Māra?
“When there is form, Rādha, there might be Māra, or a slayer, or one who dies.

Therefore, Rādha, you should see form as Māra; see it as a slayer; see it as that which dies; see it as a disease; see it as a tumor; see it as a dart; see it as a calamity; see it as a source of calamity.”
Those who see it thus see correctly.
When there is feeling...
when there is perception...
"When there are volitional formations...
when there is consciousness, there is Māra, or a killer, or one who dies.

Therefore, Rādha, you should see consciousness as Māra; see it as a killer; see it as one who dies; see it as a disease; see it as a tumor; see it as a dart; see it as a calamity; see it as a source of calamity."
“Those who see it thus, Rādha, see correctly.
“But for what purpose, venerable sir, is correct seeing?
“Correct seeing, Rādha, has the purpose of disenchantment.”
“But for what purpose, venerable sir, is disenchantment?
“Disenchantment, Rādha, has the purpose of dispassion.
“But for what purpose, venerable sir, is dispassion?”
“Dispassion, Rādha, has liberation as its purpose.
“But what, Bhante, is the purpose of liberation?
“Liberation, Rādha, has Nibbāna as its purpose.”
“But, venerable sir, for what purpose is Nibbāna?
“You have gone too far with this question, Rādha; you were not able to grasp its limit.
For, Rādha, the holy life is lived with Nibbāna as its immersion, Nibbāna as its final goal, and Nibbāna as its consummation.”
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.2 (SN 23.2, PTS SN iii 189) 1.
The First Chapter on Māra (Paṭhamamāravagga)
The Discourse on Beings.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Rādha addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“‘A being, a being,’ venerable sir, it is said.
To what extent, venerable sir, is one called ‘a being’?
“In regard to form, Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is—one is stuck there, stuck fast; therefore one is called ‘a being.’”
In regard to feeling … perception … volitional formations …
In consciousness, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is—one is attached there, thoroughly attached there; therefore one is called a "being.

Just as, Rādha, boys or girls play with sandcastles, as long as they have not lost their passion for those sandcastles, have not lost their desire, have not lost their affection, and have not lost their thirst for them...
As long as they have not departed from feverish passion and have not departed from craving, so long do those children of sand continue to cling to them,
play with them, treasure them, and treat them as "mine. But when, Rādha, those boys or girls have become free from lust for those sand-houses,
free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from feverish passion, and free from craving, then indeed those sand-houses—
With their hands and feet they scatter, disperse, demolish, and turn it into playthings.
In the same way, Rādha, you too should scatter, disperse, demolish, and turn form into a plaything; practice for the destruction of craving.
Scatter, disperse, demolish, and turn feeling into a plaything; practice for the destruction of craving.

Disperse perception, disperse it, shatter it, make it a plaything, and practice for the destruction of craving. Disperse volitional formations, disperse them, shatter them, make them a plaything, and practice for the destruction of craving.
Disperse consciousness, disperse it, shatter it, make it a plaything, and practice for the destruction of craving.
“For the destruction of craving, Rādha, is Nibbāna.
The second [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.3 (SN 23.3, PTS SN iii 190)
1. The First Chapter on Māra:
The Discourse on the Eye of Existence.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“‘The cessation of the conduit to existence, the cessation of the conduit to existence,’ it is said, Bhante.
What now, Bhante, is the conduit to existence, and what is the cessation of the conduit to existence?”
“Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, engagement, clinging, mental fixation, adherence, and underlying tendencies there are regarding form—
this is called the conduit to existence.
The cessation of these is the cessation of the conduit to existence.”
In feeling … in perception … in volitional formations …
Whatever desire there is for consciousness... [and so on] ...whatever underlying tendencies toward fixation and adherence—this is called the conduit to existence.
The cessation of these is the cessation of the conduit to existence.”
The Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.4 (SN 23.4, PTS SN iii 191) 1.
The First Chapter on Māra.
The Discourse on What is to be Fully Understood.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

The Venerable Rādha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, I will teach you the phenomena that are to be fully understood, full understanding itself, and the person who has realized full understanding.
Listen to this and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Rādha replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: “And what, Rādha, are the phenomena to be fully understood?

Form, Rādha, is a phenomenon to be fully understood; feeling is a phenomenon to be fully understood; perception is a phenomenon to be fully understood; volitional formations are phenomena to be fully understood; consciousness is a phenomenon to be fully understood.”
"These, Rādha, are called the phenomena to be fully understood.
And what, Rādha, is full understanding?
It is, Rādha, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion."
This, Rādha, is called full understanding.
And who, Rādha, is the person who has fully understood?
It should be said: "An Arahant."
“Rādha, this venerable one of such a name and such a clan—
he is called a person who has full understanding.
The fourth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.5 The First Chapter on Māra Sutta 5: The Ascetic “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics. What four? The one who is neither an ascetic nor a brahmin; the one who is an ascetic but not a brahmin; the one who is a brahmin but not an ascetic; and the one who is both an ascetic and a brahmin. And how, bhikkhus, is one neither an ascetic nor a brahmin? Here, someone does not himself live restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, yet he enjoins others to live restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. It is in this way that one is neither an ascetic nor a brahmin. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic but not a brahmin? Here, someone himself lives restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, yet he does not enjoin others to live restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. It is in this way that one is an ascetic but not a brahmin. And how, bhikkhus, is one a brahmin but not an ascetic? Here, someone himself does not live restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, yet he enjoins others to live restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. It is in this way that one is a brahmin but not an ascetic. And how, bhikkhus, is one both an ascetic and a brahmin? Here, someone himself lives restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, and he also enjoins others to live restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. It is in this way that one is both an ascetic and a brahmin. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of ascetics.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging.”
Which five?

The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, Rādha, do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging;
"Rādha, those recluses or brahmins are not, in my view, true recluses among recluses or true brahmins among brahmins;
nor do those venerable ones dwell having themselves, through direct knowledge, realized and attained for themselves in this very life the goal of the recluse or the goal of the brahmin."
But those ascetics or brahmins, Rādha, who understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five aggregates of clinging— they, Rādha,
among ascetics are accounted true ascetics and among brahmins are accounted true brahmins;
and these venerable ones, in this very life, have attained the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood.
“Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I dwell having attained it.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.6 (SN 23.6, PTS SN iii 192)
1. The First Chapter on Māra, Discourse Two on Ascetics.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Rādha, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging.
Which five?"
The form aggregate subject to clinging …pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.

For whatever ascetics or brahmins, Rādha, do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging …pe… [do not] dwell having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge.”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 23.7 (SN 23.7, PTS SN iii 192) 1.
The First Chapter on Māra (Paṭhamamāravagga)
The Discourse on Stream-Enterers. At Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, there are these five aggregates of clinging.
Which five?
The aggregate of clinging to form … [and so on] … the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.”
“Rādha, when a noble disciple understands, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging—
this, Rādha, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and headed for full enlightenment. This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.8 (SN 23.8, PTS SN iii 193) 1. Paṭhamamāravagga Arahantasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who is bound by all fetters; the one who is partly freed and partly not freed from the fetters; the one who is freed from some fetters but bound by others; and the one who is freed from all fetters. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person bound by all fetters? Here, bhikkhus, someone is not devoid of lust for the form element, not devoid of desire for it, not devoid of affection for it, not devoid of thirst for it, not devoid of passion for it, not devoid of craving for it. He is not devoid of lust for the feeling element… the perception element… the volitional formations element… the consciousness element, not devoid of desire for it, not devoid of affection for it, not devoid of thirst for it, not devoid of passion for it, not devoid of craving for it. It is in this way that one is a person bound by all fetters. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person partly freed and partly not freed from the fetters? Here, bhikkhus, someone is devoid of lust for the form element, devoid of desire for it, devoid of affection for it, devoid of thirst for it, devoid of passion for it, devoid of craving for it. But he is not devoid of lust for the feeling element… the perception element… the volitional formations element… the consciousness element, not devoid of desire for it, not devoid of affection for it, not devoid of thirst for it, not devoid of passion for it, not devoid of craving for it. It is in this way that one is a person partly freed and partly not freed from the fetters. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person freed from some fetters but bound by others? Here, bhikkhus, someone is devoid of lust for the form element, devoid of desire for it, devoid of affection for it, devoid of thirst for it, devoid of passion for it, devoid of craving for it. And he is also devoid of lust for the feeling element… the perception element… the volitional formations element… the consciousness element, devoid of desire for it, devoid of affection for it, devoid of thirst for it, devoid of passion for it, devoid of craving for it. Yet he still delights in conceptualization, finds satisfaction in conceptualization, and finds rest in conceptualization. It is in this way that one is a person freed from some fetters but bound by others. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person freed from all fetters? Here, bhikkhus, someone is devoid of lust for the form element, devoid of desire for it, devoid of affection for it, devoid of thirst for it, devoid of passion for it, devoid of craving for it. And he is also devoid of lust for the feeling element… the perception element… the volitional formations element… the consciousness element, devoid of desire for it, devoid of affection for it, devoid of thirst for it, devoid of passion for it, devoid of craving for it. Furthermore, he does not delight in conceptualization, does not find satisfaction in conceptualization, and does not find rest in conceptualization. It is in this way that one is a person freed from all fetters.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging.”
Which five?
The aggregate of clinging to form …pe… the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.

When, Rādha, a bhikkhu has understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five aggregates of clinging, he becomes liberated through non-clinging.

“Rādha, this bhikkhu is called an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right gnosis.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.9 (SN 23.9, PTS SN iii 193)
1. The First Chapter on Māra:
The Discourse on Lustful Attachment.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is regarding form—abandon that.
In this way, that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future.”
Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for feeling—that you should abandon.
In this way, that feeling will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future.
[The same applies to] perception...
Abandon whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for volitional formations.
In this way, those volitional formations will be abandoned by you, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future.
Abandon whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for consciousness.
"In this way, that consciousness will be abandoned... [and so on] ...of a nature not to arise again.
The ninth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.10 (SN 23.10, PTS SN iii 194)
1. The First Chapter on Māra:
The Second Discourse on Desire and Lust.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:

“Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are regarding form—abandon them.
In this way, that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and incapable of arising again in the future.”

Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, whatever mental fixation, adherence, and underlying tendency there is toward feeling—abandon those.
In this way, that feeling will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
[The same applies to] perception...

Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are in relation to volitional formations—abandon them.
In this way, those volitional formations will be abandoned by you, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and no longer subject to future arising.

Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are in relation to consciousness—abandon them.
"In this way, that consciousness will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Tenth. The first section on Māra from the Saṃyutta on Rādha.
Its summary verse:
Māra, a being, the conduit to existence,
the two ascetics who should be fully understood.
The stream-enterer and the arahant;
and two others [who are] beyond desire and lust.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 23.11 (SN 23.11, PTS SN iii 195)
2. The Second Chapter on Māra, Discourse on Māra.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Māra, Māra,’ it is said, Bhante.
Who, Bhante, is this Māra?”
“Form, Rādha, is Māra; feeling is Māra; perception is Māra; volitional formations are Māra; consciousness is Māra.

Seeing thus, Rādha, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands. Thus it was said.
The first.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.12. (SN 23.12, PTS SN iii 195)
2. The Second Chapter on Māra:
The Discourse on the Nature of Māra.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“‘The nature of Māra, the nature of Māra,’ it is said, Bhante.
What now, Bhante, is the nature of Māra?”
“Form, Rādha, is subject to Māra; feeling is subject to Māra; perception is subject to Māra; volitional formations are subject to Māra; consciousness is subject to Māra.
Seeing thus … he understands:
‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.13 (SN 23.13, PTS SN iii 195) 2.
The Second Chapter on Māra.
The Discourse on Impermanence.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Rādha addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘impermanent, impermanent.
Now, venerable sir, what is impermanent?
“Form, Rādha, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; mental formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent.”
"Seeing thus...
he understands: 'There is nothing further beyond this state.
The third.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.14 (SN 23.14, PTS SN iii 195) 2. The Second Chapter on Māra Aniccadhammasutta – The Discourse on Impermanent Phenomena “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Rādha said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘a thing subject to impermanence, a thing subject to impermanence.’”
“Venerable sir, what now is the nature of impermanence?

“Form, Rādha, is of the nature of impermanence; feeling is of the nature of impermanence; perception is of the nature of impermanence; mental formations are of the nature of impermanence; consciousness is of the nature of impermanence. Seeing thus … [as before] …”
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
This was the fourth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.15 (SN 23.15, PTS SN iii 196).
2. The Second Chapter on Māra:

“‘Suffering, suffering,’ it is said, venerable sir.
What now, venerable sir, is suffering?”

Fifth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.16 (SN 23.16, PTS SN iii 196) 2.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.17 (SN 23.17, PTS SN iii 196) 2. The Second Chapter on Māra The Discourse on Non-Self “Bhikkhus, form is non-self. If form were self, this body would not be subject to affliction. One could have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. But because form is non-self, this body is subject to affliction, and one cannot have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. “Feeling is non-self... Perception is non-self... Volitional formations are non-self... Consciousness is non-self. If consciousness were self, this consciousness would not be subject to affliction. One could have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness is non-self, this consciousness is subject to affliction, and one cannot have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Rādha addressed the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘Not-self, not-self.’”
“What, venerable sir, is non-self?
“Form, Rādha, is non-self; feeling is non-self; perception is non-self; volitional formations are non-self;
consciousness is non-self. Seeing thus …”
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
This is the seventh [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.18 (SN 23.18, PTS SN iii 196).

‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.’”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.20 (SN 23.20, PTS SN iii 197) 2. The Second Chapter on Māra Vayadhammasutta – The Discourse on the Nature of Decay “Bhikkhus, form is subject to decay; it is not fitting for one who knows and sees this to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Feeling is subject to decay; it is not fitting for one who knows and sees this to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Perception is subject to decay; it is not fitting for one who knows and sees this to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Volitional formations are subject to decay; it is not fitting for one who knows and sees this to regard them thus: ‘These are mine, these I am, these are my self. Consciousness is subject to decay; it is not fitting for one who knows and sees this to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.

“Venerable sir, what is subject to decay?

Seeing thus … [as before] …”
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
Thus ends the tenth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.21. (SN 23.21, PTS SN iii 197)

3. Āyācanavagga.
Mārādisuttaekādasaka.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Rādha said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Rādha, whatever is Māra—therein you should abandon desire, you should abandon lust, you should abandon desire and lust.”
And who, Rādha, is Māra?
Form, Rādha, is Māra; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Feeling is Māra; therein you should abandon desire... [and so on].
Perception is Māra; you should abandon desire for it...
Formations are Māra; you should abandon desire for them...
Consciousness is Māra; you should abandon desire for it...
“Rādha, whatever is Māra, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, abandon both desire and lust for it.
“Rādha, whatever has the nature of Māra, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, abandon both desire and lust for it...
“Rādha, whatever is impermanent... [and so on].
“Rādha, whatever is of the nature to be impermanent...
[as before] ... Rādha, whatever is suffering...
[as before] ... Rādha, whatever is of the nature to be suffering...”
“Rādha, that which is non-self … [as above] … Rādha,
that which has the nature of being non-self … [as above] … Rādha,
that which has the nature of perishing … [as above].”
“Rādha, whatever is subject to decay... [as above] ...
Rādha, whatever is subject to arising, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, abandon desire-and-lust for it...
[as above] ... *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 23.34 (SN 23.34, PTS SN iii 199)
3. Āyācanavagga.
Nirodhadhammasutta.
At Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Rādha said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Rādha, whatever is subject to cessation, you should abandon desire for it, you should abandon lust for it, you should abandon desire-and-lust for it.”
And what, Rādha, is subject to cessation?
Form, Rādha, is subject to cessation; in regard to that, desire should be abandoned.
… Feeling is subject to cessation; in regard to that, desire should be abandoned. … [and so on] …
Perception is subject to cessation; in regard to that, desire should be abandoned by you.
… Formations are subject to cessation; in regard to that, desire should be abandoned by you.
… Consciousness is subject to cessation; in regard to that, desire should be abandoned by you. …
“Rādha, whatever is subject to cessation, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, and abandon both desire and lust for it.
This concludes the third chapter, the Chapter on Entreaties.
Its summary verse:
Māra and that which is subject to Māra, two others by means of impermanence;
and two are stated by means of suffering.
Likewise with non-self;
and the arising and passing away,
and that which is subject to cessation— these are the twelve.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.35–45 (SN 23.35, PTS SN iii 200) 4. Upanisinnavagga Mārādisutta-ekādasaka (The Eleven Discourses on Māra and Others) At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is fitting for you to abandon the five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. Abandon these five hindrances, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, Ānanda, you should dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. You should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Develop these four foundations of mindfulness, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the four right strivings. What four? Here, Ānanda, you should generate desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; you should make an effort, arouse energy, apply your mind, and strive. You should generate desire for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states; you should make an effort, arouse energy, apply your mind, and strive. Develop these four right strivings, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the four bases for psychic power. What four? Here, Ānanda, you should develop the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving. You should develop the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Develop these four bases for psychic power, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Develop these five faculties, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Develop these five powers, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the seven factors of enlightenment. What seven? The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Develop these seven factors of enlightenment, Ānanda. Furthermore, Ānanda, you should develop the Noble Eightfold Path. What eight? Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Develop this Noble Eightfold Path, Ānanda. When, Ānanda, you have abandoned the five hindrances, and when you have developed the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path, then, Ānanda, you may expect to reach the supreme goal of the holy life, for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, either in this very life or after passing away.

[The Blessed One then repeated the same instructions in response to the Venerable Bhadda, the Venerable Rādha, the Venerable Anurādha, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāniputta, the Venerable Upavāna, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Nandaka, the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the Venerable Mahākassapa. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Kassapa, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is fitting for you to abandon the five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. Abandon these five hindrances, Kassapa. Furthermore, Kassapa, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness... the four right strivings... the four bases for psychic power... the five faculties... the five powers... the seven factors of enlightenment... and the Noble Eightfold Path. When, Kassapa, you have abandoned the five hindrances, and when you have developed the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path, then, Kassapa, you may expect to reach the supreme goal of the holy life, for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, either in this very life or after passing away. [The Blessed One then repeated the same instructions in response to the Venerable Mahākaccāna, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, the Venerable Mahākappina, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahāgavaccha, the Venerable Mahākāla, the Venerable Mahācūḷa, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, the Venerable Mahāpiṅgiya, the Venerable Mahākaṅkhārevata, and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Koṭṭhika, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is fitting for you to abandon the five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. Abandon these five hindrances, Koṭṭhika. Furthermore, Koṭṭhika, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness... the four right strivings... the four bases for psychic power... the five faculties... the five powers... the seven factors of enlightenment... and the Noble Eightfold Path. When, Koṭṭhika, you have abandoned the five hindrances, and when you have developed the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path, then, Koṭṭhika, you may expect to reach the supreme goal of the holy life, for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, either in this very life or after passing away. [The Blessed One then repeated the same instructions in response to the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, the Venerable Mahāpiṅgiya, the Venerable Mahākaṅkhārevata, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, the Venerable Mahācūḷa, the Venerable Mahākāla, the Venerable Mahācūḷa, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, the Venerable Mahāpiṅgiya, and the Venerable Mahāka
At Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, whatever is Māra, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, and abandon both desire and lust for it.”
And who, Rādha, is Māra?
Form, Rādha, is Māra; you should abandon desire for it...
consciousness is Māra; you should abandon desire for it...
“Rādha, whatever is Māra, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, abandon desire-and-lust for it.
“Rādha, whatever has the nature of Māra, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, abandon desire-and-lust for it...
“Rādha, whatever is impermanent... [and so on].
“Rādha, whatever is of a nature to be impermanent... [as before] ...
Rādha, whatever is suffering... [as before] ...

“Rādha, whatever is not-self …pe… Rādha,

4. Upanisinnavagga, Nirodhadhammasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Rādha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rādha, whatever is subject to cessation, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, and abandon desire-and-lust for it.
And what, Rādha, is subject to cessation?”
Form, Rādha, is subject to cessation; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Feeling … perception … [and so on] … [as above].
“Volitional formations...
consciousness is subject to cessation; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire and lust.
Whatever, Rādha, is subject to cessation—in that you must abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire and lust.”
The fourth chapter, the Upanisinnavagga.
Its summary verse: Māra and the nature of Māra.
Two others are taught by means of impermanence;
two are taught by means of suffering,
and likewise by means of non-self.
"Origination and passing away,
with cessation as their nature— these twelve.
The *Rādha Saṃyutta* is complete.
